content.rationale: The conjunction is the most fundamental and penetrating aspect. Its wide default orb of 10° reflects the classical tradition of allowing generous orb for the most concentrated aspect, particularly for luminaries. This orb may be tightened to 8° or 6° in professional practice, especially for non-luminary conjunctions.
content.narrowing_guidance: Professional astrologers often apply tighter orbs (8° or less) for body-to-body conjunctions not involving Sun or Moon. The 10° default is appropriate for beta reference; Wizard review may specify tighter orbs per planet combination.
content.source_context: Traditional Western astrology has long applied the widest orbs to the conjunction and opposition; Ptolemy and subsequent authors allowed orbs of 7–12° for the major aspects, with the conjunction receiving the widest allowance.

content.rationale: The opposition, like the conjunction, has traditionally received a generous orb given its strength and visibility in the chart. A 10° orb is consistent with classical and modern usage for the opposition.
content.narrowing_guidance: Tighter orbs (7–8°) are used in some professional traditions; the 10° default is appropriate for beta reference.
content.source_context: Classical tradition applies the same or similar orbs to the conjunction and opposition as the two most powerful aspects.

envelope.notes: Beta orb doctrine. Canonical value matches settings/astrology_settings_defaults.json.

content.rationale: The trine receives a slightly narrower orb than the conjunction and opposition, reflecting its secondary status as a major but less concentrated aspect. An 8° orb is widely used in both classical and modern practice.
content.narrowing_guidance: Some professional traditions tighten to 6–7° for body-to-body trines not involving luminaries.
content.source_context: Classical traditions assigned orbs of 7–9° to the trine; 8° is a practical middle ground consistent with most mainstream usage.

envelope.notes: Beta orb doctrine. Canonical value matches settings/astrology_settings_defaults.json.

content.rationale: The square receives the same default orb as the trine, reflecting its comparable strength as a major hard aspect. An 8° orb is consistent with mainstream modern usage.
content.narrowing_guidance: Some professional traditions tighten to 6–7° for non-luminary squares.
content.source_context: Classical and modern traditions treat the square as a major aspect comparable to the trine in strength; similar orb allowances apply.

envelope.notes: Beta orb doctrine. Canonical value matches settings/astrology_settings_defaults.json.

content.rationale: The sextile receives a moderately narrow orb relative to the major aspects, reflecting its status as a mild and somewhat less powerful aspect. A 6° orb is consistent with mainstream usage.
content.narrowing_guidance: Some professional traditions apply 4–5° for non-luminary sextiles.
content.source_context: Classical tradition assigned narrower orbs to the sextile than to the conjunction, opposition, trine, and square.

envelope.notes: Beta orb doctrine. Canonical value matches settings/astrology_settings_defaults.json.

content.rationale: The quincunx (inconjunct) is a minor aspect in most classical traditions and receives a narrow orb accordingly. The tighter orb reflects that the quincunx is primarily significant when exact or nearly exact.
content.narrowing_guidance: Many professional astrologers apply 2–3° for the quincunx; the 3° default is appropriate for beta reference.
content.source_context: The quincunx was not universally recognized in classical tradition and received narrower orbs when included in early modern practice.

envelope.notes: Beta orb doctrine. Canonical value matches settings/astrology_settings_defaults.json.

content.short_line: Default orb for minor aspects (semisextile, semisquare, sesquiquadrate, quintile, biquintile, septile, novile): 2°.
content.rationale: Minor aspects are given a narrow 2° orb to ensure that only meaningful proximity is captured. These aspects are considered secondary in most traditions and should be interpreted with restraint.
content.narrowing_guidance: Some professional practitioners apply even tighter orbs (1°) for the rarest minor aspects (septile, novile). The 2° default provides a conservative beta standard.
content.source_context: Minor aspects (quintile family, septile, novile, semisquares, etc.) were developed primarily in the 17th–20th centuries and are not universally recognized across traditions; tight orbs are standard practice.
